## Notice of Claims

Contractor shall promptly, and in no event later than five (5) Business Days, notify the Department of any Plan-related legal actions or proceedings brought or initiated against Contractor,  the  Department,  or  the  Plan,  of  which  Contractor  becomes  aware.  The Department  shall  promptly  notify  Contractor  of  any  Plan-related  legal  actions  or proceedings, brought or initiated against Contractor, the Department, or the Plan, of which the Department becomes aware.

## Department as Real Party in Interest

If a Member files suit against Contractor regarding eligibility, enrollment or coverage that is the legal administrative responsibility of the Department without previously requesting an administrative hearing pursuant to Chapter 120, Florida Statutes, Contractor shall file

a motion to dismiss or any other appropriate motions and shall notify the Department of its action. Contractor shall, when possible, notify the Department prior to the filing of such motion and shall notify the Department no later than seven (7) Business Days after the filing of any such motion. Prior to filing any such motions, Contractor shall, when possible, advise the party filing the suit, as appropriate, that issues regarding eligibility, enrollment, or coverage that is the legal administrative responsibility of the Department require the exhaustion of administrative remedies and/or in such instances the real party in interest is the  Department.  In  reference  to  legal  proceedings  regarding  eligibility,  enrollment,  or coverage that is the legal administrative responsibility of the Department, the Department may support  Contractor's  motions,  as  specified  in  this  subsection,  to  drop  Contractor and/or to substitute the Department, if the Department is not already a party to the lawsuit, as  the  real  party  in  interest  when  requested  by  Contractor.  If  the  Department  is  a codefendant in any such lawsuit, the Department may support any appropriate motion(s) to drop Contractor from the lawsuit.

## Contractor as Real Party in Interest

In the event a lawsuit is filed against Contractor, which raises a recognized cause of action or claim for relief based on Contractor's own policies or procedures to the administration of the Plan, Contractor shall, at its expense, defend such lawsuit. Contractor shall support the Department in any motion filed to drop the Department from any lawsuit where the damages sought by the filing litigant allegedly arise out of the policies and procedures of Contractor  that  do  not  concern  eligibility,  enrollment,  or  coverage  that  is  the  legal administrative responsibility of the Department.

## Cooperation in the Defense of Administrative and/or Legal Actions

The  Parties  shall,  upon  request,  cooperate  fully  with  each  other  concerning  any administrative or legal proceeding brought or initiated against them individually or jointly by Plan Enrollees or other persons relating to the administration of the Plan or Contract. In this regard, the Parties shall use their best efforts to keep each other apprised of any significant developments relating to such litigation or proceedings and the status of such legal matters as may be requested by their respective attorneys. In all administrative or legal proceedings, Contractor shall make available all files and documents requested by Department and Contractor attorneys, investigate the facts related to allegations raised in the proceedings, and make available, as required by the Department, and at no additional cost,  witnesses  for  depositions,  administrative  hearings,  and/or  trial  in  any  such proceedings.

## Administrative Proceedings

The Department, as an agency of the State, shall be responsible, in accordance with State law,  for  handling  and  defending  any  administrative  actions  or  proceedings  brought  by Members in accordance with sections 120.569, 120.57 or 120.574, Florida Statutes. Upon request, Contractor shall promptly provide the Department with all records, including but not  limited  to,  materials,  available  data,  schedules,  guidelines,  audit  trail,  protocols,  or other materials that are necessary for the preparation of the defense in such proceedings.

## Support and Communication with Contractor's Legal Affairs Department

Contractor  shall,  upon  request  of  the  Department,  assist  attorneys  representing  the Department by providing information and support in administrative and legal proceedings being contested by Members. Contractor shall advise the Department in writing within thirty (30) Calendar Days after the Effective Date of the Contract of the representative who will assist the Department's attorneys.

Subsection 10.10 shall survive termination of this Contract.

## Right of Setoff

The State may, in addition to other remedies available to it at law or equity and upon notice to Contractor, retain such monies from amounts due Contractor as may be necessary to satisfy any claim for damages, penalties, costs and the like asserted by or against the State. The State may set  off  any  liability  or  other  obligation  of  Contractor  or  its  affiliates  to  the  State  against  any payments due Contractor under any contract with the State.

Premium must be paid per the policy. The setoff of any liabilities of other Contractor entities may not be applied toward premiums for this agreement.

## Contractor's Responsibility to Notify Members

The Contractor shall, at Contractor's sole expense, notify all Members whose State of Florida Data was accessed by any Breach, unauthorized access or transmission is determined by the Department to have been caused by the Contractor or its Subcontractors no later than thirty (30) Calendar Days after the determination of a Breach or reason to believe a Breach occurred. 2|Florida Department of Management Services and State Group Insurance Program|"# Florida Department of Management Services and State Group Insurance Program

The community centers on the Florida Department of Management Services (Department), which administers the State Group Insurance Program (Plan) under a comprehensive contract with a Contractor (Awarded Respondent). The Department holds extensive oversight and enforcement rights, including audits, performance guarantees, and remedies for default. Key entities include the Contractor, Plan Participants, various compliance mechanisms, and reporting requirements. The community's structure is defined by the contract, which governs all aspects of the relationship, from service delivery to dispute resolution.

## Central Role of the Department

The Department is the central entity, serving as the contracting authority and administrator of the health insurance plan. It has final decision-making authority over benefits, claims, and contract modifications, and holds extensive enforcement and oversight rights, including conducting audits, issuing performance guarantees, and assessing financial penalties. Its broad responsibilities and authority make it the most critical entity in the community. [Data: Entities (21), Relationships (80, 90, 173, 303, 645, +more)]

## Comprehensive Contractual Framework

The Contract is the foundational legal agreement that governs all aspects of the relationship between the Department and the Contractor. It encompasses services, obligations, audits, liquidated damages, compliance requirements, and remedies for default. The Contract may only be modified upon mutual written agreement, ensuring stability and clarity. Its comprehensive nature indicates the high degree of formalization and legal complexity in this community. [Data: Entities (63), Relationships (253, 255, 256, 322, +more)]

## Detailed Performance and Compliance Mechanisms

The community includes numerous mechanisms to ensure Contractor performance, such as performance guarantees, liquidated damages, and events of default. The Department can declare an Event of Default if the Contractor's performance falls below the minimum level for three consecutive quarters, triggering remedies like termination and financial penalties. These mechanisms are designed to mitigate risks and ensure accountability. [Data: Entities (90, 114, 125, 149, 150, +more); Relationships (151, 215, 393, +more)]

## Extensive Reporting and Audit Requirements

The Contractor must submit a wide array of reports and deliverables on weekly, monthly, quarterly, and annual bases, including paid claims activity, eligibility discrepancies, and standard reporting. The Department and its designees have broad audit rights, including inspecting facilities and financial records, to verify compliance. These requirements ensure transparency and allow the Department to monitor the Contractor's performance closely. [Data: Entities (75, 353, 417, 420, 421, +more); Relationships (708, 709, 712, +more)]

## Role of Participants and Satisfaction Surveys

Participants are individuals enrolled in the Plan who receive benefits and services. Their satisfaction is monitored through annual surveys, which may trigger corrective action if performance is unsatisfactory. The Department plays a central role in overseeing these surveys and approving their instruments and reporting formats. This feedback loop helps ensure that the Plan meets the needs of its members. [Data: Entities (173, 268, 269), Relationships (325, 469, 470)]

## Contractor's Obligations and Risks

The Contractor (Awarded Respondent) is bound by the Contract to provide services, develop communications, and make programs available. It faces significant risks, including liquidated damages for untimely implementation, performance guarantees, and potential default for non-compliance. The Contractor must also adhere to specific requirements such as background checks and no offshoring of data. These obligations highlight the high stakes for the Contractor. [Data: Entities (63, 114, 218, 219), Relationships (409, 570, 571, 605, 628, +more)]

## Importance of Data Security and Privacy

The Contract includes provisions for protecting State of Florida Data, with the Department entitled to recover damages for breaches. Background checks are required for employees and subcontractors, and there are restrictions on offshoring data. These measures indicate the community's emphasis on data security and compliance with legal requirements. [Data: Entities (218, 219), Relationships (28, 80, 151, 256)]

## Dispute Resolution and Legal Proceedings

The community has formal procedures for dispute resolution, including a specific section (10.7) for resolving audit findings and equitable adjustment disputes. The Department can institute legal proceedings upon an Event of Default and is the obligee of the performance bond. These legal mechanisms provide a structured approach to resolving conflicts and enforcing contractual terms. [Data: Entities (61, 122, 90), Relationships (89, 208, 229, 151)]"

2|Florida Department of Management Services and State Group Insurance Program|"# Florida Department of Management Services and State Group Insurance Program

The community centers on the Florida Department of Management Services (Department), which administers the State Group Insurance Program (Plan) under a comprehensive contract with a Contractor (Awarded Respondent). The Department holds extensive oversight and enforcement rights, including audits, performance guarantees, and remedies for default. Key entities include the Contractor, Plan Participants, various compliance mechanisms, and reporting requirements. The community's structure is defined by the contract, which governs all aspects of the relationship, from service delivery to dispute resolution.

## Central Role of the Department

The Department is the central entity, serving as the contracting authority and administrator of the health insurance plan. It has final decision-making authority over benefits, claims, and contract modifications, and holds extensive enforcement and oversight rights, including conducting audits, issuing performance guarantees, and assessing financial penalties. Its broad responsibilities and authority make it the most critical entity in the community. [Data: Entities (21), Relationships (80, 90, 173, 303, 645, +more)]

## Comprehensive Contractual Framework

The Contract is the foundational legal agreement that governs all aspects of the relationship between the Department and the Contractor. It encompasses services, obligations, audits, liquidated damages, compliance requirements, and remedies for default. The Contract may only be modified upon mutual written agreement, ensuring stability and clarity. Its comprehensive nature indicates the high degree of formalization and legal complexity in this community. [Data: Entities (63), Relationships (253, 255, 256, 322, +more)]

## Detailed Performance and Compliance Mechanisms

The community includes numerous mechanisms to ensure Contractor performance, such as performance guarantees, liquidated damages, and events of default. The Department can declare an Event of Default if the Contractor's performance falls below the minimum level for three consecutive quarters, triggering remedies like termination and financial penalties. These mechanisms are designed to mitigate risks and ensure accountability. [Data: Entities (90, 114, 125, 149, 150, +more); Relationships (151, 215, 393, +more)]

## Extensive Reporting and Audit Requirements

The Contractor must submit a wide array of reports and deliverables on weekly, monthly, quarterly, and annual bases, including paid claims activity, eligibility discrepancies, and standard reporting. The Department and its designees have broad audit rights, including inspecting facilities and financial records, to verify compliance. These requirements ensure transparency and allow the Department to monitor the Contractor's performance closely. [Data: Entities (75, 353, 417, 420, 421, +more); Relationships (708, 709, 712, +more)]

## Role of Participants and Satisfaction Surveys

Participants are individuals enrolled in the Plan who receive benefits and services. Their satisfaction is monitored through annual surveys, which may trigger corrective action if performance is unsatisfactory. The Department plays a central role in overseeing these surveys and approving their instruments and reporting formats. This feedback loop helps ensure that the Plan meets the needs of its members. [Data: Entities (173, 268, 269), Relationships (325, 469, 470)]

## Contractor's Obligations and Risks

The Contractor (Awarded Respondent) is bound by the Contract to provide services, develop communications, and make programs available. It faces significant risks, including liquidated damages for untimely implementation, performance guarantees, and potential default for non-compliance. The Contractor must also adhere to specific requirements such as background checks and no offshoring of data. These obligations highlight the high stakes for the Contractor. [Data: Entities (63, 114, 218, 219), Relationships (409, 570, 571, 605, 628, +more)]

## Importance of Data Security and Privacy

The Contract includes provisions for protecting State of Florida Data, with the Department entitled to recover damages for breaches. Background checks are required for employees and subcontractors, and there are restrictions on offshoring data. These measures indicate the community's emphasis on data security and compliance with legal requirements. [Data: Entities (218, 219), Relationships (28, 80, 151, 256)]

## Dispute Resolution and Legal Proceedings

The community has formal procedures for dispute resolution, including a specific section (10.7) for resolving audit findings and equitable adjustment disputes. The Department can institute legal proceedings upon an Event of Default and is the obligee of the performance bond. These legal mechanisms provide a structured approach to resolving conflicts and enforcing contractual terms. [Data: Entities (61, 122, 90), Relationships (89, 208, 229, 151)]"

2|Florida Department of Management Services and State Group Insurance Program|"# Florida Department of Management Services and State Group Insurance Program

The community centers on the Florida Department of Management Services (Department), which administers the State Group Insurance Program (Plan) under a comprehensive contract with a Contractor (Awarded Respondent). The Department holds extensive oversight and enforcement rights, including audits, performance guarantees, and remedies for default. Key entities include the Contractor, Plan Participants, various compliance mechanisms, and reporting requirements. The community's structure is defined by the contract, which governs all aspects of the relationship, from service delivery to dispute resolution.

## Central Role of the Department

The Department is the central entity, serving as the contracting authority and administrator of the health insurance plan. It has final decision-making authority over benefits, claims, and contract modifications, and holds extensive enforcement and oversight rights, including conducting audits, issuing performance guarantees, and assessing financial penalties. Its broad responsibilities and authority make it the most critical entity in the community. [Data: Entities (21), Relationships (80, 90, 173, 303, 645, +more)]

## Comprehensive Contractual Framework

The Contract is the foundational legal agreement that governs all aspects of the relationship between the Department and the Contractor. It encompasses services, obligations, audits, liquidated damages, compliance requirements, and remedies for default. The Contract may only be modified upon mutual written agreement, ensuring stability and clarity. Its comprehensive nature indicates the high degree of formalization and legal complexity in this community. [Data: Entities (63), Relationships (253, 255, 256, 322, +more)]

## Detailed Performance and Compliance Mechanisms

The community includes numerous mechanisms to ensure Contractor performance, such as performance guarantees, liquidated damages, and events of default. The Department can declare an Event of Default if the Contractor's performance falls below the minimum level for three consecutive quarters, triggering remedies like termination and financial penalties. These mechanisms are designed to mitigate risks and ensure accountability. [Data: Entities (90, 114, 125, 149, 150, +more); Relationships (151, 215, 393, +more)]

## Extensive Reporting and Audit Requirements

The Contractor must submit a wide array of reports and deliverables on weekly, monthly, quarterly, and annual bases, including paid claims activity, eligibility discrepancies, and standard reporting. The Department and its designees have broad audit rights, including inspecting facilities and financial records, to verify compliance. These requirements ensure transparency and allow the Department to monitor the Contractor's performance closely. [Data: Entities (75, 353, 417, 420, 421, +more); Relationships (708, 709, 712, +more)]

## Role of Participants and Satisfaction Surveys

Participants are individuals enrolled in the Plan who receive benefits and services. Their satisfaction is monitored through annual surveys, which may trigger corrective action if performance is unsatisfactory. The Department plays a central role in overseeing these surveys and approving their instruments and reporting formats. This feedback loop helps ensure that the Plan meets the needs of its members. [Data: Entities (173, 268, 269), Relationships (325, 469, 470)]

## Contractor's Obligations and Risks

The Contractor (Awarded Respondent) is bound by the Contract to provide services, develop communications, and make programs available. It faces significant risks, including liquidated damages for untimely implementation, performance guarantees, and potential default for non-compliance. The Contractor must also adhere to specific requirements such as background checks and no offshoring of data. These obligations highlight the high stakes for the Contractor. [Data: Entities (63, 114, 218, 219), Relationships (409, 570, 571, 605, 628, +more)]

## Importance of Data Security and Privacy

The Contract includes provisions for protecting State of Florida Data, with the Department entitled to recover damages for breaches. Background checks are required for employees and subcontractors, and there are restrictions on offshoring data. These measures indicate the community's emphasis on data security and compliance with legal requirements. [Data: Entities (218, 219), Relationships (28, 80, 151, 256)]

## Dispute Resolution and Legal Proceedings

The community has formal procedures for dispute resolution, including a specific section (10.7) for resolving audit findings and equitable adjustment disputes. The Department can institute legal proceedings upon an Event of Default and is the obligee of the performance bond. These legal mechanisms provide a structured approach to resolving conflicts and enforcing contractual terms. [Data: Entities (61, 122, 90), Relationships (89, 208, 229, 151)]"

The Department holds extensive enforcement and oversight rights, including conducting performance and compliance audits of the Contractor and Subcontractors, inspecting facilities and background screening processes, performing periodic performance reviews, issuing performance guarantees, and assessing financial penalties and liquidated damages. 7|Capital Health Plan and the State of Florida ITN HMO Contract|"# Capital Health Plan and the State of Florida ITN HMO Contract

The community centers on Capital Health Plan (CHP), an HMO and Independent Licensee of the Blue Cross and Blue Shield Association, which submitted a response to an Invitation to Negotiate (ITN) issued by the State of Florida Department of Management Services for HMO Fully-Insured, Carve-Out Performance Guarantees. CHP proposed medical loss ratio guarantees and offers various plans such as HDHP, Commercial Standard, and fully-insured HMO options. The community includes CHP's extensive network of subcontractors for services like HEDIS auditing, interpretation, telehealth, and disease management, as well as regulatory entities like the Department and program stakeholders such as primary care physicians, specialists, and subscribers. The structure is oriented around CHP's contractual obligations to provide healthcare services and manage disease management programs, with financial and compliance implications for the State of Florida.

## Capital Health Plan's Central Role and Procurement Participation

Capital Health Plan (CHP) is the pivotal entity in this community, functioning as a health maintenance organization (HMO) and an Independent Licensee of the Blue Cross and Blue Shield Association. CHP submitted a response to the Invitation to Negotiate (ITN) issued by the State of Florida, demonstrating its active engagement in competitive procurement processes for state-level health plan services. The ITN, specifically for HMO Fully-Insured, Carve-Out Performance Guarantees, serves as the solicitation document to which CHP responded. CHP's proposal includes medical loss ratio guarantees, where it would issue rebates to the State of Florida if the actual MLR falls below a 95% target, and rate guarantees for 2024-2026, ensuring firm rates with specified caps. These commitments underscore CHP's financial and operational obligations. [Data: Entities (391, 450, 64, 461, 448, 449); Relationships (655, 750, 770)]

## Extensive Subcontractor Network Supporting CHP's Operations

CHP relies on a diverse network of subcontracted vendors to deliver various healthcare services and administrative functions. Notable subcontractors include Healthy People, a HEDIS audit firm; Language Line Solutions for interpretation services; AIM Specialty Health for radiation benefits management; Amwell, Inc. for urgent care and telehealth; BCBS of Florida for Blue Card Network and anti-fraud investigation; and several others like HealthTrio LLC for IT services and Healthwise Inc. for shared decision-making tools. These subcontractors are integral to CHP's ability to fulfill its contractual obligations, providing specialized expertise and support. The relationships are direct and well-documented, with CHP as the central coordinator. [Data: Entities (541, 542, 533, 534, 535, 536, 537, 538, 539, 540); Relationships (889, 890, 881, 882, 883, 884, 885, 886, 887, 888)]

## Disease Management Program and Stakeholder Engagement

CHP operates a comprehensive disease management program that includes bundled disease management, nurse management, and opt-out enrollment. The program involves multiple stakeholders: the Associate Medical Director of Clinical Quality oversees the program, approves new initiatives, and monitors outcomes; disease management staff, including 7 experienced RNs, conduct outreach and refer patients internally; and primary care physicians (PCPs) are notified and engaged when patients enroll. High-risk patients may be referred to the Nancy Van Vessem, MD, Center for Healthy Aging for evaluation. The program coordinates with pharmacy management and behavioral health services, and uses tools like DxCG algorithms for risk stratification and the patient portal and nurse coach for secure communication. This integrated approach aims to manage chronic conditions and improve health outcomes. [Data: Entities (339, 403, 545, 546, 547, 543, 544, 530, 529, 531, 532); Relationships (867, 894, 895, 896, 891, 892, 868, 869, 872, 873)]

## Regulatory and Compliance Framework

The community is subject to significant regulatory oversight, primarily from the State of Florida Department of Management Services, which issued the ITN. The Department is responsible for annual filings such as the Retiree Drug Subsidy (RDS) and requires data from the insurer. The contract resulting from the ITN includes specific requirements, such as restrictions on transfer or sale of equity interests or assets, and a 16-month period following termination. CHP must also comply with network adequacy standards, ensuring that subscribers have access to primary care physicians within specified distances in suburban (8 miles) and rural (15 miles) areas. Additionally, the Clinical/Medical Management Activities and Outcomes Report is a quarterly report of utilization, cost, and savings associated with clinical programs like case management, utilization management, and disease management. These compliance elements highlight the formal and legal nature of the relationships. [Data: Entities (64, 454, 323, 328, 330, 329, 407, 408); Relationships (658, 763, 565, 567, 566, 689, 690)]

## Provider Network and Access Requirements

CHP, as the Respondent, is obligated to maintain a network of participating physicians and hospitals, including primary care physicians, specialists, obstetricians/gynecologists, pediatricians, and hospitals, to provide services under the plan. The network must meet accessibility standards: in suburban areas, 95% of subscribers must have access to at least two primary care physicians within 8 miles of their home zip code, and in rural areas, 95% of subscribers must have access to at least one primary care physician within 15 miles. These requirements ensure that subscribers have adequate access to care. The network also includes pharmacies, with various commercial retail networks and drug lists such as COM Retail Network and Comm Open Preferred Drug, which are associated with CHP. [Data: Entities (401, 404, 405, 406, 242, 407, 408, 550, 551, 552); Relationships (673, 681, 682, 683, 684, 685, 689, 690, 901, 902, 903)]

## Financial Guarantees and Plan Offerings

CHP's proposal includes financial guarantees such as a medical loss ratio (MLR) guarantee and rate guarantees. The MLR guarantee stipulates that CHP would issue rebates to the State of Florida if the actual MLR falls below 95%, and it covers combined Commercial Standard and HDHP plans. Rate guarantees apply to the years 2024-2026, ensuring that proposed rates will remain firm and not exceed specified caps. CHP offers various health plan options, including a fully-insured HMO, HDHP, and Medicare Retiree plans through Employer Group Waiver Plans (EGWP). These financial commitments and plan designs are critical to the contract's value and risk profile. [Data: Entities (450, 461, 448, 449, 452, 451, 458, 453, 455); Relationships (750, 770, 748, 754, 753, 775, 777)]

## Quality Measurement and Audit

CHP utilizes the Healthcare Effectiveness Data and Information Set (HEDIS) as a quality measurement tool to track performance on relevant healthcare measures. Healthy People, a HEDIS audit firm subcontracted by CHP, provides oversight of this quality measurement tool. The plan tracks performance on HEDIS indicators for specific populations, such as the diabetic disease management population, which shows favorable efficiency scores due to lower rates of avoidable rescue care. This focus on quality measurement and audit ensures accountability and continuous improvement in care delivery. [Data: Entities (541, 525, 526, 558, 579); Relationships (889, 878)]"

Upon becoming aware of an alleged Breach or Incident, the Contractor shall set up  a  conference  call  (via  a  telephone  call  and  email)  with  the  Department's Contract Manager and any necessary parties. The conference call invitation shall contain a brief description of the nature of the event. When possible, a thirty (30) minute notice shall be given to allow Department personnel to be available for the call. If the designated time is not practical for the Department, an alternate time for the call shall be scheduled. All available information shall be shared on the call. The Contractor shall answer all questions based on the information known at that time  and  shall  answer  additional  questions  as  additional  information  becomes known. The Contractor shall provide the Department with final documentation of the incident including all actions that took place. If the Contractor becomes aware of  a  Breach  or  Incident  outside  of  normal  business  hours,  the  Contractor  shall notify the Department's Contract Manager as soon as possible, and in all events, within twenty-four (24) hours.

The Contractor's failure to perform the obligations in this subsection shall also be an Event of Default, and will entitle the Department to recover any other damages it incurs arising from a failure to perform the obligations in this subsection (including any actual out-of-pocket expenses incurred by the Department to investigate and remediate the violation) and/or to pursue injunctive relief.

## Contractor's Responsibility to Notify Members

The Contractor shall, at Contractor's sole expense, notify all Members whose State of Florida Data was accessed by any Breach, unauthorized access or transmission is determined by the Department to have been caused by the Contractor or its Subcontractors no later than thirty (30) Calendar Days after the determination of a Breach or reason to believe a Breach occurred. If the

Contractor cannot identify the specific persons whose data may have been accessed,  such  notice  shall  be  provided  to  all  persons  whose  data reasonably may have been accessed. The Department shall pay all costs to notify such persons related to any Breach determined by the Department to not have been caused by the Contractor or its Subcontractors. Nothing in this subsection will alter or replace the application of section 501.171, Florida Statutes,  as  to  the  Contractor's  obligations  and  liability  for  Breaches concerning confidential personal information.

## Credit Monitoring and Notification

The Contractor  shall  include  credit  monitoring  services  at  its  own  cost  for those Members affected or potentially affected by an alleged Breach for no less than a period of one (1) year following the Breach.

The Contractor shall provide the Department of Legal Affairs written notice of a Breach that affects 500 or more Members as soon as practicable, but not later than thirty (30) Calendar Days after the determination of the Breach or reason to believe a Breach has occurred. The Contractor shall provide the Department a copy of the written notice to the Department of Legal Affairs. If a Breach impacts more than 1,000 Members at a single time, the Contractor shall notify, without unreasonable delay, all consumer reporting agencies that compile and maintain files on consumers on a nationwide basis, as defined in the Fair Credit Reporting Act, 15 U.S. Code Section 1681a (p), of the timing, distribution,  and  content  of  the  notices  required  pursuant  to  Contract subsections 4.2.5.2 ('Contractor's Responsibility to Notify Department') and 4.2.5.3.1 ('Contractor's Responsibility to Notify Members') of this Contract.

## Duty to Provide Secure Data

The Contractor will maintain the security of State of Florida Data including, but not limited to, a secure area around any display of such State of Florida Data or State of Florida Data that is otherwise visible. 7|Capital Health Plan and the State of Florida ITN HMO Contract|"# Capital Health Plan and the State of Florida ITN HMO Contract

The community centers on Capital Health Plan (CHP), an HMO and Independent Licensee of the Blue Cross and Blue Shield Association, which submitted a response to an Invitation to Negotiate (ITN) issued by the State of Florida Department of Management Services for HMO Fully-Insured, Carve-Out Performance Guarantees. CHP proposed medical loss ratio guarantees and offers various plans such as HDHP, Commercial Standard, and fully-insured HMO options. The community includes CHP's extensive network of subcontractors for services like HEDIS auditing, interpretation, telehealth, and disease management, as well as regulatory entities like the Department and program stakeholders such as primary care physicians, specialists, and subscribers. The structure is oriented around CHP's contractual obligations to provide healthcare services and manage disease management programs, with financial and compliance implications for the State of Florida.

## Capital Health Plan's Central Role and Procurement Participation

Capital Health Plan (CHP) is the pivotal entity in this community, functioning as a health maintenance organization (HMO) and an Independent Licensee of the Blue Cross and Blue Shield Association. CHP submitted a response to the Invitation to Negotiate (ITN) issued by the State of Florida, demonstrating its active engagement in competitive procurement processes for state-level health plan services. The ITN, specifically for HMO Fully-Insured, Carve-Out Performance Guarantees, serves as the solicitation document to which CHP responded. CHP's proposal includes medical loss ratio guarantees, where it would issue rebates to the State of Florida if the actual MLR falls below a 95% target, and rate guarantees for 2024-2026, ensuring firm rates with specified caps. These commitments underscore CHP's financial and operational obligations. [Data: Entities (391, 450, 64, 461, 448, 449); Relationships (655, 750, 770)]

## Extensive Subcontractor Network Supporting CHP's Operations

CHP relies on a diverse network of subcontracted vendors to deliver various healthcare services and administrative functions. Notable subcontractors include Healthy People, a HEDIS audit firm; Language Line Solutions for interpretation services; AIM Specialty Health for radiation benefits management; Amwell, Inc. for urgent care and telehealth; BCBS of Florida for Blue Card Network and anti-fraud investigation; and several others like HealthTrio LLC for IT services and Healthwise Inc. for shared decision-making tools. These subcontractors are integral to CHP's ability to fulfill its contractual obligations, providing specialized expertise and support. The relationships are direct and well-documented, with CHP as the central coordinator. [Data: Entities (541, 542, 533, 534, 535, 536, 537, 538, 539, 540); Relationships (889, 890, 881, 882, 883, 884, 885, 886, 887, 888)]

## Disease Management Program and Stakeholder Engagement

CHP operates a comprehensive disease management program that includes bundled disease management, nurse management, and opt-out enrollment. The program involves multiple stakeholders: the Associate Medical Director of Clinical Quality oversees the program, approves new initiatives, and monitors outcomes; disease management staff, including 7 experienced RNs, conduct outreach and refer patients internally; and primary care physicians (PCPs) are notified and engaged when patients enroll. High-risk patients may be referred to the Nancy Van Vessem, MD, Center for Healthy Aging for evaluation. The program coordinates with pharmacy management and behavioral health services, and uses tools like DxCG algorithms for risk stratification and the patient portal and nurse coach for secure communication. This integrated approach aims to manage chronic conditions and improve health outcomes. [Data: Entities (339, 403, 545, 546, 547, 543, 544, 530, 529, 531, 532); Relationships (867, 894, 895, 896, 891, 892, 868, 869, 872, 873)]

## Regulatory and Compliance Framework

The community is subject to significant regulatory oversight, primarily from the State of Florida Department of Management Services, which issued the ITN. The Department is responsible for annual filings such as the Retiree Drug Subsidy (RDS) and requires data from the insurer. The contract resulting from the ITN includes specific requirements, such as restrictions on transfer or sale of equity interests or assets, and a 16-month period following termination. CHP must also comply with network adequacy standards, ensuring that subscribers have access to primary care physicians within specified distances in suburban (8 miles) and rural (15 miles) areas. Additionally, the Clinical/Medical Management Activities and Outcomes Report is a quarterly report of utilization, cost, and savings associated with clinical programs like case management, utilization management, and disease management. These compliance elements highlight the formal and legal nature of the relationships. [Data: Entities (64, 454, 323, 328, 330, 329, 407, 408); Relationships (658, 763, 565, 567, 566, 689, 690)]

## Provider Network and Access Requirements

CHP, as the Respondent, is obligated to maintain a network of participating physicians and hospitals, including primary care physicians, specialists, obstetricians/gynecologists, pediatricians, and hospitals, to provide services under the plan. The network must meet accessibility standards: in suburban areas, 95% of subscribers must have access to at least two primary care physicians within 8 miles of their home zip code, and in rural areas, 95% of subscribers must have access to at least one primary care physician within 15 miles. These requirements ensure that subscribers have adequate access to care. The network also includes pharmacies, with various commercial retail networks and drug lists such as COM Retail Network and Comm Open Preferred Drug, which are associated with CHP. [Data: Entities (401, 404, 405, 406, 242, 407, 408, 550, 551, 552); Relationships (673, 681, 682, 683, 684, 685, 689, 690, 901, 902, 903)]

## Financial Guarantees and Plan Offerings

CHP's proposal includes financial guarantees such as a medical loss ratio (MLR) guarantee and rate guarantees. The MLR guarantee stipulates that CHP would issue rebates to the State of Florida if the actual MLR falls below 95%, and it covers combined Commercial Standard and HDHP plans. Rate guarantees apply to the years 2024-2026, ensuring that proposed rates will remain firm and not exceed specified caps. CHP offers various health plan options, including a fully-insured HMO, HDHP, and Medicare Retiree plans through Employer Group Waiver Plans (EGWP). These financial commitments and plan designs are critical to the contract's value and risk profile. [Data: Entities (450, 461, 448, 449, 452, 451, 458, 453, 455); Relationships (750, 770, 748, 754, 753, 775, 777)]

## Quality Measurement and Audit

CHP utilizes the Healthcare Effectiveness Data and Information Set (HEDIS) as a quality measurement tool to track performance on relevant healthcare measures. Healthy People, a HEDIS audit firm subcontracted by CHP, provides oversight of this quality measurement tool. The plan tracks performance on HEDIS indicators for specific populations, such as the diabetic disease management population, which shows favorable efficiency scores due to lower rates of avoidable rescue care. This focus on quality measurement and audit ensures accountability and continuous improvement in care delivery. [Data: Entities (541, 525, 526, 558, 579); Relationships (889, 878)]"

2|Florida Department of Management Services and State Group Insurance Program|"# Florida Department of Management Services and State Group Insurance Program

The community centers on the Florida Department of Management Services (Department), which administers the State Group Insurance Program (Plan) under a comprehensive contract with a Contractor (Awarded Respondent). The Department holds extensive oversight and enforcement rights, including audits, performance guarantees, and remedies for default. Key entities include the Contractor, Plan Participants, various compliance mechanisms, and reporting requirements. The community's structure is defined by the contract, which governs all aspects of the relationship, from service delivery to dispute resolution.

## Central Role of the Department

The Department is the central entity, serving as the contracting authority and administrator of the health insurance plan. It has final decision-making authority over benefits, claims, and contract modifications, and holds extensive enforcement and oversight rights, including conducting audits, issuing performance guarantees, and assessing financial penalties. Its broad responsibilities and authority make it the most critical entity in the community. [Data: Entities (21), Relationships (80, 90, 173, 303, 645, +more)]

## Comprehensive Contractual Framework

The Contract is the foundational legal agreement that governs all aspects of the relationship between the Department and the Contractor. It encompasses services, obligations, audits, liquidated damages, compliance requirements, and remedies for default. The Contract may only be modified upon mutual written agreement, ensuring stability and clarity. Its comprehensive nature indicates the high degree of formalization and legal complexity in this community. [Data: Entities (63), Relationships (253, 255, 256, 322, +more)]

## Detailed Performance and Compliance Mechanisms

The community includes numerous mechanisms to ensure Contractor performance, such as performance guarantees, liquidated damages, and events of default. The Department can declare an Event of Default if the Contractor's performance falls below the minimum level for three consecutive quarters, triggering remedies like termination and financial penalties. These mechanisms are designed to mitigate risks and ensure accountability. [Data: Entities (90, 114, 125, 149, 150, +more); Relationships (151, 215, 393, +more)]

## Extensive Reporting and Audit Requirements

The Contractor must submit a wide array of reports and deliverables on weekly, monthly, quarterly, and annual bases, including paid claims activity, eligibility discrepancies, and standard reporting. The Department and its designees have broad audit rights, including inspecting facilities and financial records, to verify compliance. These requirements ensure transparency and allow the Department to monitor the Contractor's performance closely. [Data: Entities (75, 353, 417, 420, 421, +more); Relationships (708, 709, 712, +more)]

## Role of Participants and Satisfaction Surveys

Participants are individuals enrolled in the Plan who receive benefits and services. Their satisfaction is monitored through annual surveys, which may trigger corrective action if performance is unsatisfactory. The Department plays a central role in overseeing these surveys and approving their instruments and reporting formats. This feedback loop helps ensure that the Plan meets the needs of its members. [Data: Entities (173, 268, 269), Relationships (325, 469, 470)]

## Contractor's Obligations and Risks

The Contractor (Awarded Respondent) is bound by the Contract to provide services, develop communications, and make programs available. It faces significant risks, including liquidated damages for untimely implementation, performance guarantees, and potential default for non-compliance. The Contractor must also adhere to specific requirements such as background checks and no offshoring of data. These obligations highlight the high stakes for the Contractor. [Data: Entities (63, 114, 218, 219), Relationships (409, 570, 571, 605, 628, +more)]

## Importance of Data Security and Privacy

The Contract includes provisions for protecting State of Florida Data, with the Department entitled to recover damages for breaches. Background checks are required for employees and subcontractors, and there are restrictions on offshoring data. These measures indicate the community's emphasis on data security and compliance with legal requirements. [Data: Entities (218, 219), Relationships (28, 80, 151, 256)]

## Dispute Resolution and Legal Proceedings

The community has formal procedures for dispute resolution, including a specific section (10.7) for resolving audit findings and equitable adjustment disputes. The Department can institute legal proceedings upon an Event of Default and is the obligee of the performance bond. These legal mechanisms provide a structured approach to resolving conflicts and enforcing contractual terms. [Data: Entities (61, 122, 90), Relationships (89, 208, 229, 151)]"
4|Eligibility Discrepancy Report and Its Components|"# Eligibility Discrepancy Report and Its Components

The community centers on the Eligibility Discrepancy Report, a weekly report that aggregates three sub-reports: the Duplicate Records Report, the Reject Records Report, and the Address Errors Report. These components are directly linked to the main report, indicating a hierarchical structure where the Eligibility Discrepancy Report serves as the parent entity. The community is focused on data quality and error tracking within eligibility processes.

## Eligibility Discrepancy Report as the central entity

The Eligibility Discrepancy Report is the core entity in this community, acting as the primary weekly report that consolidates data quality issues. It has a high degree of connectivity, with relationships to three component reports. This central role suggests it is the key output for monitoring and addressing eligibility discrepancies, which are critical for accurate and efficient eligibility determinations. The report's comprehensive nature allows stakeholders to identify and rectify issues such as duplicate records, rejected records, and address errors in a timely manner. [Data: Entities (310); Relationships (548, 549, 550)]

## Duplicate Records Report as a component

The Duplicate Records Report is a specialized sub-report that focuses on identifying duplicate entries within eligibility data. As a component of the Eligibility Discrepancy Report, it contributes to the overall goal of maintaining data integrity. Duplicate records can lead to overpayments, underpayments, or other administrative inefficiencies, making this report essential for operational accuracy. Its direct relationship with the main report highlights its importance in the weekly reporting cycle. [Data: Entities (311); Relationships (548)]

## Reject Records Report as a component

The Reject Records Report is another critical component that documents records that have been rejected due to various errors or inconsistencies. This report helps in identifying systemic issues in data submission or processing, enabling corrective actions. By being part of the Eligibility Discrepancy Report, it ensures that rejected records are reviewed and addressed promptly, reducing the risk of delays or inaccuracies in eligibility determinations. [Data: Entities (312); Relationships (549)]

## Address Errors Report as a component

The Address Errors Report specifically targets discrepancies related to addresses, which are fundamental for contacting individuals and verifying eligibility. Errors in addresses can result in miscommunication, failed notifications, and incorrect eligibility statuses. As a component of the weekly Eligibility Discrepancy Report, this sub-report facilitates the correction of address data, thereby improving the overall quality of the eligibility system. [Data: Entities (313); Relationships (550)]

## Hierarchical structure of the community

The community exhibits a clear hierarchical structure, with the Eligibility Discrepancy Report as the parent entity and the three sub-reports as its children. This structure is defined by the relationships where the main report 'includes' each component. Such an organization enables a systematic approach to error tracking, where each sub-report addresses a specific type of discrepancy, and the main report provides a consolidated view. This hierarchical model is efficient for management and resolution of data quality issues. [Data: Relationships (548, 549, 550)]

## Limited scope and low connectivity

The community consists of only four entities and three relationships, indicating a narrow scope focused solely on the weekly reporting mechanism. The low connectivity, with each component linked only to the main report and not to each other, suggests that the sub-reports operate independently but are aggregated for comprehensive analysis. This limited scope implies that the community's impact is confined to internal data management processes, with no external entities or broader implications evident from the provided data. [Data: Entities (310, 311, 312, 313); Relationships (548, 549, 550)]"

0|Awarded Respondent: Contracted Plan Administrator|"# Awarded Respondent: Contracted Plan Administrator

The community is centered on the Awarded Respondent, a vendor contracted by the Department to administer a health plan. The Awarded Respondent is responsible for a wide range of administrative, operational, and reporting tasks, including claims processing, coordination of benefits, member services, and compliance with performance standards. It collaborates with various entities such as PEOPLE FIRST for eligibility updates, Medicare third-party administrators, and an Independent Review Organization for appeals. The Department oversees the contract, and the Awarded Respondent must provide extensive reporting and data to ensure accountability. Key relationships illustrate the Awarded Respondent's obligation to report on plan types (Standard, Health Investor), subgroups (Active, Retirees), and wellness programs, as well as its duty to comply with audit and regulatory requirements.

## Central Role of the Awarded Respondent

The Awarded Respondent is the pivotal entity in this community, contracted by the Department to provide comprehensive administrative services for a health plan. Its responsibilities encompass claims processing, coordination of benefits, customer service, and compliance with numerous performance standards. The Awarded Respondent must implement all contract requirements, including the Implementation Plan, and is subject to performance guarantees, operational milestones, liquidated damages, and staffing obligations. It operates the Customer Service Unit and Plan website, develops and distributes Plan materials, and provides data and reports to the Department on a regular basis. This central role makes the Awarded Respondent essential to the functioning of the health plan and the community. [Data: Entities (195); Relationships (368, 496, 497, 498, 499, +more)]

## Extensive Reporting Obligations

The Awarded Respondent is required to submit a wide array of reports to the Department, covering areas such as performance standards, claims summaries, fraud and waste, renewal, and key metrics. These reports are submitted on weekly, monthly, quarterly, semi-annual, and annual bases, ensuring ongoing oversight and accountability. For example, the Performance Standards Guarantee Report is delivered quarterly, the Paid Claims Summary Report monthly, and the Fraud, Abuse and Waste Report quarterly. Additionally, the Awarded Respondent must provide reporting data categorized by plan type (including Health Investor and Standard) and by subgroup (Active, Retirees Under 65, Retirees 65 and Over). This extensive reporting framework underscores the Awarded Respondent's accountability to the Department and the importance of data-driven oversight. [Data: Entities (306, 307, 308, 309, 317, +more); Relationships (542, 543, 544, 545, 554, +more)]

## Coordination with External Entities

The Awarded Respondent collaborates with several external entities to fulfill its contractual duties. PEOPLE FIRST provides eligibility updates, including manual reinstatements and terminations, to the Awarded Respondent. Medicare's third-party administrators coordinate with the Awarded Respondent for claims processing as primary and secondary payers, and the Awarded Respondent resolves Medicare Secondary Payer notices to avoid offsets. An Independent Review Organization (IRO) conducts external reviews as part of the appeals process. These collaborations are critical for ensuring accurate and timely processing of benefits and appeals. [Data: Entities (267, 277, 290); Relationships (466, 484, 499, 513)]

## Compliance and Audit Requirements

The Awarded Respondent is subject to rigorous compliance and audit requirements to ensure adherence to contract provisions. It must submit to an annual audit of contractual compliance and provide audit access to 100% of claims data, utilization management reviews, clinical program outcomes, and appeals. The Awarded Respondent also agrees to the audit provisions of Contract Section 5. Failure to submit data properly may result in penalties under PG 15 and PG 18. Additionally, the Awarded Respondent must develop and implement Corrective Action Plans when survey questions fall below standard, addressing any missed performance standards. These compliance measures are designed to maintain high standards of accountability and transparency. [Data: Entities (344, 355, 356, 357, 358, +more); Relationships (546, 609, 610, 611, 612, +more)]

## Member Services and Communication

The Awarded Respondent is responsible for developing and distributing a variety of Plan materials to members, including Summaries of Material Modifications, Summaries of Benefits and Coverage, member educational materials, identification cards, benefit brochures, claim forms, and provider directories. It must provide an online directory of network providers and mailed directories upon request. The Awarded Respondent also operates customer service and call center operations, handles appeals, and provides Explanation of Benefits Statements. Moreover, it must provide Plan materials in a culturally and linguistically appropriate manner as defined by section 2719 of the PHSA. These services ensure that members have access to necessary information and support. [Data: Entities (227, 228, 229, 230, 231, +more); Relationships (419, 420, 421, 422, 423, +more)]

## Wellness Program Reporting

The Awarded Respondent reports on various components of a wellness program, including Health Risk Assessments, biometric screenings, coaching programs, online tools, challenges, and onsite programs. It must report on activity, participation, and aggregate results for these components, as well as member satisfaction. For instance, the Awarded Respondent reports HRA activity, participation, and aggregate results, and reports on coaching program participation and outcomes. This reporting helps the Department assess the effectiveness of wellness initiatives. [Data: Entities (333, 334, 335, 336, 337, +more); Relationships (581, 582, 583, 584, 585, +more)]

## Post-Termination Responsibilities

The Awarded Respondent has obligations that extend beyond the contract term. It must continue to process run-out claims (claims incurred through the contract expiration date) for a 16-month period following termination. During this period, it must also provide mailroom services, appeals services, and system/technical services. These post-termination duties ensure continuity of care for plan participants and a smooth transition to a subsequent awarded respondent. [Data: Entities (372, 373, 375, 376, 377); Relationships (631, 632, 633, 634, 635)]

## Performance Standards and Penalties

The Awarded Respondent is held to strict performance standards, with penalties for non-compliance. It must be 100% operational by January 1, 2024, and mail ID cards to participants by December 15, 2023, or ten business days after receipt of the eligibility file. Failure to meet performance standards can result in the requirement to submit a Corrective Action Plan and may trigger penalties under PG 15 and PG 18 for data submission failures. These measures incentivize timely and accurate performance. [Data: Entities (212, 213); Relationships (391, 394, 500, 501, 546)]

## Contractual and Financial Oversight

The Awarded Respondent must adhere to contractual provisions regarding invoicing, payment, and financial accountability. It must complete a direct deposit authorization form as required by the Department of Financial Services and follow the invoicing requirements specified in the contract. The Department must approve all Plan materials and communications, and the Awarded Respondent requires approval for changes. Additionally, the Awarded Respondent provides the Performance Bond and Insurance Report to the Department for verification of sufficient coverage and bond for each calendar year. These financial and contractual oversights ensure proper use of funds and compliance with legal requirements. [Data: Entities (345, 367, 368); Relationships (368, 592, 627, 629)]

## Provider Network Requirements

The Awarded Respondent is required to own at least 80% of its proposed provider network within the State. The provider network is evaluated as part of the subscriber satisfaction survey. The Awarded Respondent must provide an online and mailed provider directory that is updated in real time. It must also report on network provider additions and deletions by city/state, county, and specialty on a quarterly basis. These requirements ensure that members have access to a robust network of providers. [Data: Entities (332, 320, 244); Relationships (569, 557, 440)]"

More broadly, an Event of Default may include triggering occurrences such as insolvency, placement on a vendor list, suspension, felony conviction, refusal of access, offshoring violations, or failure to meet performance standards. Such an occurrence entitles the non-defaulting party to specified remedies.

Events of Default are not limited to Contractor failures. An Event of Default may also be an occurrence on the part of the Department, which entitles the Contractor to remedies including equitable relief and monetary damages. In addition, an Event of Default occurs when the Contractor fails to perform its obligations under the Breach notification subsection, entitling the Department to damages and injunctive relief. ## Disqualifying Offenses

If at any time it is determined that a Person has a criminal misdemeanor or felony record regardless of  adjudication (e.g., adjudication withheld, a plea of guilty or

nolo contendere, or a guilty verdict) within the last six (6) years from the date of the court's determination for the crimes listed below, or their equivalent in any jurisdiction, the Contractor is required to immediately remove that Person from any position with Access to State of Florida Data or directly performing services under the Contract. The disqualifying offenses are:

- (a)  Computer-related crimes;
- (b)  Information technology crimes;
- (c)  Fraudulent practices;
- (d)  False pretenses;
- (e)  Frauds;
- (f) Credit card crimes;
- (g)  Forgery;
- (h)  Counterfeiting;
- (i) Violations involving checks or drafts;
- (j) Misuse of medical or personnel records;
- (k)  Felony theft; and
- (l) Identity Theft.

If the Contractor finds a Disqualifying Offense for a Person within the last six (6) years from the date of the court's disposition, it may obtain information regarding the  incident  and  determine  whether  that  Person  should  continue  providing Services  under  the  Contract  or  have  Access  to  State  of  Florida  Data.  The Contractor will consider the following factors only in making the determination: i.) nature and gravity of the offense, ii.) the amount of time that lapsed since the offense, iii.) the rehabilitation efforts of the person and iv.) relevancy of the offense to the job duties of the Person. If the Contractor determines that the Person should be allowed Access to State of Florida Data, then Contractor shall maintain all criminal background screening information and the rationale for such Access in the Person's employment file.

The Contractor shall require all Persons to self-report within three (3) Business Days of adjudication to the Contractor any adjudication of guilt as described above for  the  Disqualifying  Offenses. The  Contractor  shall  immediately  disallow  that Person Access to any State of Florida Data or from directly performing Services under  the  Contract.    Additionally,  the  Contractor  shall  require  that  the  Person complete an annual certification that he or she has not received an adjudication of guilt  as  described  above  for  the  Disqualifying  Offenses  and  shall  maintain  that certification in the employment file.

## Refresh Screening

The Contractor will ensure that all background screening will be refreshed every five (5) years from the time initially performed for each Person during the term of the Contract.

Department will have the right to inspect the Contractor's working area, computer systems, and/or location upon two (2) Business Days prior written

notice to the Contractor to ensure that Access to the State of Florida Data is secure and in compliance with the Contract and all applicable state and federal rules and regulations.

## Record Retention

The Contractor shall retain a list of all Persons with Access to State of Florida Data, including a statement confirming that each Person has passed the Background Screening required herein. Such a statement shall not include the substance of the screening results, only that the Person has passed the screening.

The Contractor shall create a written policy for the protection of State of Florida Data, including a policy and procedure for Access to State of Florida Data.

The Contractor shall document and record, with respect to each instance of Access to State of Florida Data:

- 1) The identity of all individual(s) who Accessed State of Florida Data in any way, whether those individuals are authorized Persons or not;
- 2) The duration of the individual(s)' Access to State of Florida Data, including the time and date at which the Access began and ended;
- 3) The identity, form, and extent of State of Florida Data accessed, including, but  not  limited  to,  whether  the  individual  Accessed  partial  or  redacted versions of State of Florida Data, read-only versions of State of Florida Data, or editable versions of State of Florida Data; and
- 4) The nature of the Access to State of Florida Data, including whether State of Florida Data was edited or shared with any other individual or entity during the duration of the Access, and, if so, the identity of the individual or entity.

The Contractor shall retain the written policy and information required in this subsection for the duration of this Contract and a period of no less than five (5)  years  from  the  date  of  termination  of  this  Contract  and  any  Contract extensions. 2|Florida Department of Management Services and State Group Insurance Program|"# Florida Department of Management Services and State Group Insurance Program

The community centers on the Florida Department of Management Services (Department), which administers the State Group Insurance Program (Plan) under a comprehensive contract with a Contractor (Awarded Respondent). The Department holds extensive oversight and enforcement rights, including audits, performance guarantees, and remedies for default. Key entities include the Contractor, Plan Participants, various compliance mechanisms, and reporting requirements. The community's structure is defined by the contract, which governs all aspects of the relationship, from service delivery to dispute resolution.

## Central Role of the Department

## Defense of Third-Party Claims

## Notice of Claims

Contractor shall promptly, and in no event later than five (5) Business Days, notify the Department of any Plan-related legal actions or proceedings brought or initiated against Contractor,  the  Department,  or  the  Plan,  of  which  Contractor  becomes  aware. ## Department as Real Party in Interest

If a Member files suit against Contractor regarding eligibility, enrollment or coverage that is the legal administrative responsibility of the Department without previously requesting an administrative hearing pursuant to Chapter 120, Florida Statutes, Contractor shall file

a motion to dismiss or any other appropriate motions and shall notify the Department of its action. Contractor shall, when possible, notify the Department prior to the filing of such motion and shall notify the Department no later than seven (7) Business Days after the filing of any such motion. Prior to filing any such motions, Contractor shall, when possible, advise the party filing the suit, as appropriate, that issues regarding eligibility, enrollment, or coverage that is the legal administrative responsibility of the Department require the exhaustion of administrative remedies and/or in such instances the real party in interest is the  Department.  In  reference  to  legal  proceedings  regarding  eligibility,  enrollment,  or coverage that is the legal administrative responsibility of the Department, the Department may support  Contractor's  motions,  as  specified  in  this  subsection,  to  drop  Contractor and/or to substitute the Department, if the Department is not already a party to the lawsuit, as  the  real  party  in  interest  when  requested  by  Contractor.  If  the  Department  is  a codefendant in any such lawsuit, the Department may support any appropriate motion(s) to drop Contractor from the lawsuit.

## Contractor as Real Party in Interest

In the event a lawsuit is filed against Contractor, which raises a recognized cause of action or claim for relief based on Contractor's own policies or procedures to the administration of the Plan, Contractor shall, at its expense, defend such lawsuit. Contractor shall support the Department in any motion filed to drop the Department from any lawsuit where the damages sought by the filing litigant allegedly arise out of the policies and procedures of Contractor  that  do  not  concern  eligibility,  enrollment,  or  coverage  that  is  the  legal administrative responsibility of the Department.

In this regard, the Parties shall use their best efforts to keep each other apprised of any significant developments relating to such litigation or proceedings and the status of such legal matters as may be requested by their respective attorneys. In all administrative or legal proceedings, Contractor shall make available all files and documents requested by Department and Contractor attorneys, investigate the facts related to allegations raised in the proceedings, and make available, as required by the Department, and at no additional cost,  witnesses  for  depositions,  administrative  hearings,  and/or  trial  in  any  such proceedings.

## Administrative Proceedings

The Department, as an agency of the State, shall be responsible, in accordance with State law,  for  handling  and  defending  any  administrative  actions  or  proceedings  brought  by Members in accordance with sections 120.569, 120.57 or 120.574, Florida Statutes. 2|Florida Department of Management Services and State Group Insurance Program|"# Florida Department of Management Services and State Group Insurance Program

The community centers on the Florida Department of Management Services (Department), which administers the State Group Insurance Program (Plan) under a comprehensive contract with a Contractor (Awarded Respondent). The Department holds extensive oversight and enforcement rights, including audits, performance guarantees, and remedies for default. Key entities include the Contractor, Plan Participants, various compliance mechanisms, and reporting requirements. The community's structure is defined by the contract, which governs all aspects of the relationship, from service delivery to dispute resolution.

## Central Role of the Department

The Department is the central entity, serving as the contracting authority and administrator of the health insurance plan. It has final decision-making authority over benefits, claims, and contract modifications, and holds extensive enforcement and oversight rights, including conducting audits, issuing performance guarantees, and assessing financial penalties. Its broad responsibilities and authority make it the most critical entity in the community. [Data: Entities (21), Relationships (80, 90, 173, 303, 645, +more)]

## Comprehensive Contractual Framework

The Contract is the foundational legal agreement that governs all aspects of the relationship between the Department and the Contractor. It encompasses services, obligations, audits, liquidated damages, compliance requirements, and remedies for default. The Contract may only be modified upon mutual written agreement, ensuring stability and clarity. Its comprehensive nature indicates the high degree of formalization and legal complexity in this community. [Data: Entities (63), Relationships (253, 255, 256, 322, +more)]

## Detailed Performance and Compliance Mechanisms

The community includes numerous mechanisms to ensure Contractor performance, such as performance guarantees, liquidated damages, and events of default. The Department can declare an Event of Default if the Contractor's performance falls below the minimum level for three consecutive quarters, triggering remedies like termination and financial penalties. These mechanisms are designed to mitigate risks and ensure accountability. [Data: Entities (90, 114, 125, 149, 150, +more); Relationships (151, 215, 393, +more)]

## Extensive Reporting and Audit Requirements

The Contractor must submit a wide array of reports and deliverables on weekly, monthly, quarterly, and annual bases, including paid claims activity, eligibility discrepancies, and standard reporting. The Department and its designees have broad audit rights, including inspecting facilities and financial records, to verify compliance. These requirements ensure transparency and allow the Department to monitor the Contractor's performance closely. [Data: Entities (75, 353, 417, 420, 421, +more); Relationships (708, 709, 712, +more)]

## Role of Participants and Satisfaction Surveys

Participants are individuals enrolled in the Plan who receive benefits and services. Their satisfaction is monitored through annual surveys, which may trigger corrective action if performance is unsatisfactory. The Department plays a central role in overseeing these surveys and approving their instruments and reporting formats. This feedback loop helps ensure that the Plan meets the needs of its members. [Data: Entities (173, 268, 269), Relationships (325, 469, 470)]

## Contractor's Obligations and Risks

The Contractor (Awarded Respondent) is bound by the Contract to provide services, develop communications, and make programs available. It faces significant risks, including liquidated damages for untimely implementation, performance guarantees, and potential default for non-compliance. The Contractor must also adhere to specific requirements such as background checks and no offshoring of data. These obligations highlight the high stakes for the Contractor. [Data: Entities (63, 114, 218, 219), Relationships (409, 570, 571, 605, 628, +more)]

## Importance of Data Security and Privacy

The Contract includes provisions for protecting State of Florida Data, with the Department entitled to recover damages for breaches. Background checks are required for employees and subcontractors, and there are restrictions on offshoring data. These measures indicate the community's emphasis on data security and compliance with legal requirements. [Data: Entities (218, 219), Relationships (28, 80, 151, 256)]

## Dispute Resolution and Legal Proceedings

The community has formal procedures for dispute resolution, including a specific section (10.7) for resolving audit findings and equitable adjustment disputes. The Department can institute legal proceedings upon an Event of Default and is the obligee of the performance bond. These legal mechanisms provide a structured approach to resolving conflicts and enforcing contractual terms. [Data: Entities (61, 122, 90), Relationships (89, 208, 229, 151)]"

If at any time it is determined that a Person has a criminal misdemeanor or felony record regardless of  adjudication (e.g., adjudication withheld, a plea of guilty or

- (a)  Computer-related crimes;
- (b)  Information technology crimes;
- (c)  Fraudulent practices;
- (d)  False pretenses;
- (e)  Frauds;
- (f) Credit card crimes;
- (g)  Forgery;
- (h)  Counterfeiting;
- (i) Violations involving checks or drafts;

- (k)  Felony theft; and

If the Contractor finds a Disqualifying Offense for a Person within the last six (6) years from the date of the court's disposition, it may obtain information regarding the  incident  and  determine  whether  that  Person  should  continue  providing Services  under  the  Contract  or  have  Access  to  State  of  Florida  Data. 2|Florida Department of Management Services and State Group Insurance Program|"# Florida Department of Management Services and State Group Insurance Program

The community centers on the Florida Department of Management Services (Department), which administers the State Group Insurance Program (Plan) under a comprehensive contract with a Contractor (Awarded Respondent). The Department holds extensive oversight and enforcement rights, including audits, performance guarantees, and remedies for default. Key entities include the Contractor, Plan Participants, various compliance mechanisms, and reporting requirements. The community's structure is defined by the contract, which governs all aspects of the relationship, from service delivery to dispute resolution.

## Central Role of the Department

The Department is the central entity, serving as the contracting authority and administrator of the health insurance plan. It has final decision-making authority over benefits, claims, and contract modifications, and holds extensive enforcement and oversight rights, including conducting audits, issuing performance guarantees, and assessing financial penalties. Its broad responsibilities and authority make it the most critical entity in the community. [Data: Entities (21), Relationships (80, 90, 173, 303, 645, +more)]

The Contract may only be modified upon mutual written agreement, ensuring stability and clarity. Its comprehensive nature indicates the high degree of formalization and legal complexity in this community. [Data: Entities (63), Relationships (253, 255, 256, 322, +more)]

The community includes numerous mechanisms to ensure Contractor performance, such as performance guarantees, liquidated damages, and events of default. The Department can declare an Event of Default if the Contractor's performance falls below the minimum level for three consecutive quarters, triggering remedies like termination and financial penalties. More broadly, an Event of Default may include triggering occurrences such as insolvency, placement on a vendor list, suspension, felony conviction, refusal of access, offshoring violations, or failure to meet performance standards. Events of Default are not limited to Contractor failures. ## Disqualifying Offenses

If at any time it is determined that a Person has a criminal misdemeanor or felony record regardless of  adjudication (e.g., adjudication withheld, a plea of guilty or

nolo contendere, or a guilty verdict) within the last six (6) years from the date of the court's determination for the crimes listed below, or their equivalent in any jurisdiction, the Contractor is required to immediately remove that Person from any position with Access to State of Florida Data or directly performing services under the Contract. The disqualifying offenses are:

- (a)  Computer-related crimes;
- (b)  Information technology crimes;
- (c)  Fraudulent practices;
- (d)  False pretenses;
- (e)  Frauds;
- (f) Credit card crimes;
- (g)  Forgery;
- (h)  Counterfeiting;
- (i) Violations involving checks or drafts;
- (j) Misuse of medical or personnel records;
- (k)  Felony theft; and
- (l) Identity Theft.

If the Contractor finds a Disqualifying Offense for a Person within the last six (6) years from the date of the court's disposition, it may obtain information regarding the  incident  and  determine  whether  that  Person  should  continue  providing Services  under  the  Contract  or  have  Access  to  State  of  Florida  Data.  The Contractor will consider the following factors only in making the determination: i.) nature and gravity of the offense, ii.) the amount of time that lapsed since the offense, iii.) the rehabilitation efforts of the person and iv.) relevancy of the offense to the job duties of the Person. If the Contractor determines that the Person should be allowed Access to State of Florida Data, then Contractor shall maintain all criminal background screening information and the rationale for such Access in the Person's employment file.

The Contractor shall require all Persons to self-report within three (3) Business Days of adjudication to the Contractor any adjudication of guilt as described above for  the  Disqualifying  Offenses. The  Contractor  shall  immediately  disallow  that Person Access to any State of Florida Data or from directly performing Services under  the  Contract.    Additionally,  the  Contractor  shall  require  that  the  Person complete an annual certification that he or she has not received an adjudication of guilt  as  described  above  for  the  Disqualifying  Offenses  and  shall  maintain  that certification in the employment file.

- 3)  Premiums: The Department shall not be responsible for any premiums or assessments on the bond.
